units.label: Multithreading — many threads on one core
units.src: A(h3("Multithreading — many threads on one core"))

units.label: A single core often stalls (waiting for memory or a cac
units.src: A(p("A single core often stalls (waiting for memory or a cache miss). Multithreading lets one " "core hold several threads at once and switch to another when one stalls, so the functional units " "stay busy. There are three classic flavours."))

A(table(["Type","How it switches","Key idea"], [["Fine-grained (interleaved)","Every clock cycle, round-robin between threads","Hides short stalls; needs many threads; each thread runs slowly"], ["Coarse-grained","Switch only on a long stall (e.g. a cache miss)","Cheap to add; the new thread needs time to refill its pipeline"], ["Simultaneous multithreading (SMT)","Issue instructions from several threads in the same cycle","Best use of a superscalar core's issue slots; appears as “hyper-threading”"]], widths=[1.5,2.2,2.3]))

A(bullets([ "Fetch — read the instruction at address PC from memory; increment PC.", "Decode — work out what the instruction means and which registers it needs.", "Execute — perform the operation in the ALU.", "Memory — access data memory (only for load/store).", "Write-back — store the result in a register.", ]))

A(h1(2,"Measuring Performance: CPU Time, CPI, MIPS & Amdahl's Law","The single most examined numerical topic"))

units.label: Performance is about time. The only true measure
units.src: A(p("Performance is about time. The only true measure of a computer's speed is how long a real " "program takes to run. But to reason about why one machine is faster, we break that time into " "parts we can measure and change. This section builds the performance equation from scratch, because " "almost every numerical question in the papers uses it."))

units.label: 2.1 Response time vs throughput
units.src: A(h3("2.1 Response time vs throughput"))

A(table(["Concept","Definition","How you improve it"],
      [["Response (execution) time","Time between the start and the completion of one task.","Faster clock, lower CPI, fewer instructions."],
       ["Throughput","Total work done per unit time (e.g. tasks per second).","More cores / more parallelism, better overlap (pipelining)."]],
      widths=[1.3,3.2,2.0]))

A(callout("Classic distinction: adding processors usually improves throughput but not the response " "time of a single task. Pipelining improves throughput without shortening the latency of one task."))

units.label: 2.2 The performance equation (the master formula)
units.src: A(h3("2.2 The performance equation (the master formula)"))

units.label: A program's execution time depends on three things, and
units.src: A(p("A program's execution time depends on three things, and they multiply:"))

A(formula("CPU Time = Instruction Count (IC) × CPI × Clock Cycle Time\n"
              "CPU Time = (IC × CPI) / Clock Frequency"))

A(table(["Term","Meaning","Units"], [["IC (Instruction Count)","Number of instructions the program executes.","instructions"], ["CPI","Average Cycles Per Instruction = total cycles / IC.","cycles per instruction"], ["Clock Cycle Time (CCT)","Duration of one clock period, CCT = 1 / f.","seconds (or ns)"], ["Clock Frequency (f)","Number of cycles per second.","Hz (GHz = 109 Hz)"]], widths=[1.7,3.5,1.3]))

units.label: Because different instruction types cost different numb
units.src: A(p("Because different instruction types cost different numbers of cycles, the average CPI is a " "weighted average of the CPI of each class:"))

A(formula("CPI = Σ (CPIᵢ × Fᵢ) ,   where Fᵢ = fraction (or share) of instructions of class i,  Σ Fᵢ = 1\n"
              "Equivalently  CPI = (Σ CPIᵢ × countᵢ) / IC"))

label: 2.3 Deriving the equation (why it is a product)

units.label: 2.3 Deriving the equation (why it is a product)
units.src: A(h3("2.3 Deriving the equation (why it is a product)"))

units.label: <ast.Constant object at 0x705cb9331610>
units.src: A(fig("page028.jpg", w=10.5*gen.cm, cap="CPU-time and CPI worked examples from the lecture notes (source: p. 28)."))

units.label: Reading the figure. These are the worked CPU-tim
units.src: A(p("Reading the figure. These are the worked CPU-time examples from the notes. Follow how IC, CPI and clock period multiply to give total time, and how the instruction mix turns into an average CPI — this is exactly the calculation the paper asks for."))

units.label: Suppose a program has IC instructions. On averag
units.src: A(p("Suppose a program has IC instructions. On average each instruction takes CPI clock " "cycles. So the total number of clock cycles is IC × CPI. Each cycle lasts CCT seconds. " "Multiplying gives the total time. This is why the three factors are independent levers: you can " "reduce any one of them to speed up the program."))
A(callout("Trap: reducing instruction count may raise CPI (e.g. CISC), and raising clock speed may " "raise CPI (deeper pipeline). The three factors are not independent in real designs.", 'warn'))

units.label: 2.4 MIPS — million instructions per second
units.src: A(h3("2.4 MIPS — million instructions per second"))
A(formula("MIPS = IC / (Execution Time × 10⁶) = f / (CPI × 10⁶)"))

units.label: MIPS measures how many millions of instructions
units.src: A(p("MIPS measures how many millions of instructions are executed each second. It is easy to quote " "but dangerous to trust, because:"))

A(bullets([ "It does not account for what an instruction does — a machine with tiny instructions looks fast.", "It varies between programs on the same machine (different instruction mixes).", "It ignores I/O and memory behaviour.", "It can be used only to compare machines with the same ISA.", ]))
A(callout("Memory hook: MIPS is meaningless across different ISAs. Use CPU time for fair " "comparisons. (This is exactly the point of PYQ ca1/ca19.)", 'warn'))

units.label: 2.5 Speed-up and Amdahl's Law
units.src: A(h3("2.5 Speed-up and Amdahl's Law"))

units.label: <ast.Constant object at 0x705cb9338510>
units.src: A(fig("page019.jpg", w=10.0*gen.cm, cap="Deriving Amdahl's law and the effect of the serial part (source: p. 19)."))

units.label: Reading the figure. The derivation of Amdahl's l
units.src: A(p("Reading the figure. The derivation of Amdahl's law. The time is split into the enhanced fraction f and the unenhanced fraction (1−f). As the enhancement factor k grows, the speed-up saturates at 1/(1−f) — the serial part sets the ceiling."))

units.label: Amdahl's Law answers: <i>“If I speed up part of the mac
units.src: A(p("Amdahl's Law answers: “If I speed up part of the machine, how much faster does the whole program " "get?” The answer is limited by the part you did not speed up."))

A(formula("Speed-up S = Old execution time / New execution time = T<sub>old</sub> / T<sub>new</sub>\n"
              "Amdahl:  S = 1 / [ (1 − f) + f / k ]\n"
              "   f = fraction of the original time that is enhanced (0 ≤ f ≤ 1)\n"
              "   k = speed-up of the enhanced portion (k > 1)"))

units.label: Derivation. Let the original time be 1 unit. The
units.src: A(p("Derivation. Let the original time be 1 unit. The enhanced fraction f is sped up by a " "factor k, so it now takes f/k. The unenhanced fraction (1 − f) is unchanged. The new " "total time is (1 − f) + f/k. The speed-up is the ratio of old to new: 1 / [(1 − f) + f/k]."))

label: 2.6 The ceiling: the serial fraction limits everything

units.label: 2.6 The ceiling: the serial fraction limits everything
units.src: A(h3("2.6 The ceiling: the serial fraction limits everything"))

units.label: As k → ∞ (the enhanced part becomes infinitely fast), t
units.src: A(p("As k → ∞ (the enhanced part becomes infinitely fast), the speed-up tends to a hard ceiling:"))

A(formula("Maximum speed-up = 1 / (1 − f)   as k → ∞\n"
              "If 10% of the code cannot be parallelised (1 − f = 0.1), the maximum speed-up is 1/0.1 = 10× — "
              "no matter how many processors you add."))
A(callout("Interpreting f: in parallel-speedup problems, f is the parallelisable fraction and " "k is the number of processors P. Then S = 1 / [(1 − f) + f/P].", 'tip'))

label: 2.7 Amdahl with a slowdown elsewhere (trade-off version)

units.label: 2.7 Amdahl with a slowdown elsewhere (trade-off version)
units.src: A(h3("2.7 Amdahl with a slowdown elsewhere (trade-off version)"))

units.label: <ast.Constant object at 0x705cb933b110>
units.src: A(fig("page020.jpg", w=10.5*gen.cm, cap="Deriving the performance/Amdahl relationships from first principles (source: p. 20)."))

units.label: Reading the figure. The same algebra written out
units.src: A(p("Reading the figure. The same algebra written out for the general case, showing why a fixed serial fraction caps the achievable speed-up no matter how much you improve the parallel part."))

units.label: Real design changes can slow down other parts. I
units.src: A(p("Real design changes can slow down other parts. If enhancing one part speeds it by k₁ but " "slows another fraction by k₂ (k₂ < 1 means slower), extend the law to add the slowed fraction:"))

A(formula("T<sub>new</sub> = (1 − f₁ − f₂) + f₁/k₁ + f₂/k₂ ,   S = 1 / T<sub>new</sub>\n"
              "f₁ = fraction enhanced, k₁ = its speed-up;  f₂ = fraction slowed, k₂ = its speed factor"))

units.label: After the change, the new share of a component i
units.src: A(p("After the change, the new share of a component is its new time divided by the new total time. " "The relative importance of components shifts, which is why a second enhancement may be less " "valuable than it first appears (PYQ ca36)."))

units.src: A(h3("2.10 Design constraints: power, thermal and the multicore shift"))

Dennard scaling ended around 2005: power density started rising " "with each shrink, so clock frequency could no longer increase freely. Designers turned to " "multicore (more cores at moderate frequency) and to power-aware techniques instead."))

A(bullets([ "Never compare MIPS across ISAs; compare CPU time.", "CPI is an average — always weight by the fraction of each instruction class.", "Amdahl's Law always has the form 1 / (unimproved + improved). Identify f first, then plug in.", "Speed-up = old/new; “X% faster” means new = old/(1+X/100).", "Watch units: GHz = 10⁹ Hz; convert cycles to time with CCT = 1/f.", "A “65% improvement” in AMAT means the new AMAT is 35% of the old (see PYQ ca15/ca26).", ]))

units.label: Previous-Year Questions — Performance & Amdahl
units.src: A(h3("Previous-Year Questions — Performance & Amdahl"))
A(Paragraph("Q (ca3 · Q2). Derive and explain Amdahl's law.", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. Let a program take time T. A fraction f of that time can be enhanced; " "the enhancement makes that fraction k times faster. The unenhanced part (1−f)T is unchanged. New time " "= (1−f)T + (fT)/k. Speed-up S = T / new time = 1/[(1−f) + f/k]. As k→∞, S→1/(1−f): the serial part " "sets the ceiling.", ST['ans']))
A(formula("T_new = (1−f)T + (fT)/k ;   S = 1 / [(1−f) + f/k] ;   S_max = 1/(1−f)"))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca4 · Q1). A program has a portion enhanced to run 4× faster, giving a system speed-up "
      "of 3.3×. What is the fraction enhanced?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Answer: f ≈ 92.9% of the original time must be in the enhanced portion.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca4 · Q2). A quad-core could speed up a computer by 4×, but rarely does. Use Amdahl to "
      "find the percentage of execution that must be parallelised for overall speed-ups of 3, 2, 1.5, 1.25.", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Answer: to gain 3× you must parallelise ~88.9%; for 2× ~66.7%; for 1.5× ~44.4%; for " "1.25× ~26.7%. Notice how quickly the required parallel fraction grows.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca4 · Q3). A benchmark: 39% loads, 12% stores, 28% ALU, 6% multiplies, 2% divides, 10% "
      "conditional branches, 3% unconditional branches. CPIs: loads/stores 5, ALU 3, multiply 6, divide 15, "
      "branch 4. Which single ALU enhancement is best?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Answer: (d) — improving the ALU (non-multiply/divide) gives the largest CPI " "reduction (0.28), because ALU operations are the most frequent.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca5 · Q4 / ca19 · Q1). MIPS ISA at 500 MHz: ALU 3 cycles, branch/jump 2, sw 4, lw 5. A "
      "program executes 200M ALU, 55M branch/jump, 25M sw and 20M lw. Find the CPU time.", ST['q']))

A(formula("IC = 200M + 55M + 25M + 20M = 300M instructions\n"
              "Total cycles = 200M×3 + 55M×2 + 25M×4 + 20M×5\n"
              "             = 600M + 110M + 100M + 100M = 910M cycles\n"
              "T_clock = 1/500 MHz = 2 ns\n"
              "CPU time = 910M × 2 ns = 1820 ms = 1.82 s"))
A(Paragraph("Answer: CPU time = 1.82 s (CPI = 910M/300M ≈ 3.03).", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca7 · Q1a). Amdahl with communication overhead. (a) Speed-up with 8 processors if, for "
      "every processor added, communication overhead is 0.5% of the original execution time. (b) Speed-up "
      "with N processors if, each time the number of processors doubles, the overhead increases by 0.5%.", ST['q']))

A(formula("(a) With P processors, serial part s, parallel part (1−s), plus overhead 0.5%×(P−1):\n"
              "    T_new = s + (1−s)/P + 0.005(P−1)   (times the original time)\n"
              "    For P=8: S = 1 / [ s + (1−s)/8 + 0.005×7 ] = 1/[ s + (1−s)/8 + 0.035 ]\n"
              "    (substitute the given serial fraction s).\n"
              "(b) With N processors, overhead = 0.005×log₂N:\n"
              "    S(N) = 1 / [ s + (1−s)/N + 0.005·log₂N ]"))

A(Paragraph("Idea being tested: communication overhead grows with the number of processors, so " "speed-up saturates and can even fall — this is the practical limit Amdahl's plain form ignores.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca33 · Q1). Three modification versions affect components X, Y, Z whose execution-time "
      "fractions are 30%, 45%, 25%. Given each version's speed factors, find the overall speed-up of each and "
      "rank them.", ST['q']))

A(formula("S_version = 1 / [ 0.30/k_X + 0.45/k_Y + 0.25/k_Z ]\n"
              "(read k_X,k_Y,k_Z from the table for each version; k<1 means slower)"))

A(Paragraph("Method: evaluate the weighted sum for each version, take the reciprocal, then rank " "from largest S. A component that is slowed (k<1) increases its term and can pull S below 1.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca36 · Q1a). (i) A new FP unit speeds FP by 2×; FP is 20% of execution time — overall "
      "speed-up? (ii) The change also slows data-cache accesses by 1.5× (2/3 speed-up); data-cache accesses "
      "are 10% of time — overall speed-up now? (iii) What % of the new execution time is FP, and what % is "
      "data cache?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Answer: (i) 1.11×; (ii) 1.05× (the cache slowdown eats most of the gain); (iii) FP " "≈ 10.5%, data cache ≈ 15.8% of the new time.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca36 · Q1b). Vector hardware makes a computation 10× faster; the measured vectorisation "
      "is 70%. What vectorisation would be needed to equal a further 2× speed-up of the vector unit (i.e. 20× "
      "total)?", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Answer: the compiler team would need only ≈66.3% vectorisation (actually less " "than the current 70%) — meaning the current vectorisation already beats the proposed 2× hardware " "speed-up. State the comparison explicitly.", ST['ans']))

A(h1(3,"Instruction Set Architecture: RISC vs CISC","The hardware/software contract"))

units.label: The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the co
units.src: A(p("The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the complete set of instructions, registers, " "addressing modes and data types that a processor understands. It is the interface between " "hardware and software: the compiler targets the ISA, and the hardware implements it. Two programs " "written for the same ISA run on every processor of that family, no matter how differently the " "hardware is built."))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca25 · Q2). For the loop below, what are the contents of the ROB when we have issued all "
                "instructions in the loop twice, assuming the L.D and S.D of the first iteration have "
                "committed and all other instructions have completed execution?", ST['q']))

A(formula("Loop: L.D    F0, 0(R1)   ; F0 = array element\n"
              "      ADD.D  F4, F0, F2   ; add scalar in F2\n"
              "      S.D    F4, 0(R1)    ; store result\n"
              "      DADDUI R1, R1, #-8  ; decrement pointer\n"
              "      BNE    R1, R2, Loop ; branch"))

A(Paragraph("Solution. Issuing the loop twice gives 10 instructions. The first iteration's L.D and " "S.D have committed (left the ROB); every other instruction has completed execution " "but is still waiting to commit (or, for the branch, has resolved). So the ROB holds the " "completed-but-uncommitted entries in program order: ADD.D(F4), DADDUI(R1), BNE, then the " "second iteration's L.D(F0), ADD.D(F4), S.D(F4), DADDUI(R1), BNE — each with its computed " "value, marked ready, and flagged speculative where it lies past a branch that has not " "committed.", ST['ans']))

       ["3 (S.D F4,0(R1))","iter 1","Yes","Committed → left the ROB"],
       ["4 DADDUI R1,R1,#-8","iter 1","Yes","Waiting"],
       ["5 BNE R1,R2,Loop","iter 1","Yes","Waiting (resolved)"],
       ["6 L.D F0,0(R1)","iter 2","Yes","Waiting"],
       ["7 ADD.D F4,F0,F2","iter 2","Yes","Waiting"],
       ["8 S.D F4,0(R1)","iter 2","Yes","Waiting"],
       ["9 DADDUI R1,R1,#-8","iter 2","Yes","Waiting"],

A(Paragraph("Q (ca28 · Q4c). How is Tomasulo's algorithm modified to include speculation? What additional "
                "hardware is required?", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. Add a Reorder Buffer and a commit stage. Instructions allocate " "ROB entries in order at issue; results are written to the ROB and broadcast on the CDB; the " "ROB supplies operands to waiting instructions and the register file is only updated at " "commit, in program order. Branch prediction directs which path is fetched; on a " "misprediction the ROB is flushed past the branch. Additional hardware: the ROB itself (with " "valid/ready/speculative bits), logic to handle ROB head commit, branch-prediction hardware, " "and flush/recovery logic. This yields precise exceptions and correct recovery from " "mispredicted branches.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca40 · Q3d). Discuss the role of Tomasulo's algorithm in out-of-order execution, with an "

A(Paragraph("Q (ca28 · Q4a,b). (a) Distinguish between static and dynamic scheduling. (b) Name three major "
      "techniques that reduce control-hazard stalls and explain them.", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Solution.", ST['ans']))

A(bullets([ "(a) Static scheduling decides the instruction order at compile time (no run-time information); " "dynamic scheduling reorders instructions in hardware at run time using reservation stations and can " "react to cache misses and variable latencies.", "(b) (1) Branch prediction — guess the direction and fetch down that path, flushing only " "on a misprediction. (2) Delayed branch — the compiler places a useful instruction in the branch " "delay slot so it always executes. (3) Branch Target Buffer — cache the branch's target and " "direction so fetching continues with no penalty on a hit. (Speculation with a reorder buffer is a " "fourth.)", ]))
A(Paragraph("Q (ca34 · Q1a). State the advantages of out-of-order pipelines over in-order pipelines.", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. An out-of-order (OOO) pipeline can execute independent instructions while " "a slow instruction (e.g. a cache-missing load or a long FP divide) waits, so it keeps functional units " "busy and achieves a lower effective CPI. In-order pipelines must stall the whole pipe behind the slow " "instruction. OOO also adapts to run-time events (misses, variable latencies) that a static schedule " "cannot see. The cost is extra hardware: reservation stations, a reorder buffer, and complex issue " "logic.", ST['ans']))

Count distinct " "blocks touched (M's instructions, S's instructions, the two data words) and how many times each is " "evicted and refetched.", "(iii) Evictions: an eviction happens when a new block maps to a line already occupied by a " "different block. Transitions: I→E on an exclusive read miss; E→M on a local write; M→S on " "a snooped read (supply data + write back); S→I on a snooped invalidate.", ]))

      widths=[1.4,2.4,2.2]))
A(Paragraph("Q (ca3 · Q4). What is virtual memory? Explain the need for virtual memory.", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. Virtual memory lets each program use a large, contiguous virtual address " "space that is mapped to physical memory by a page table. It is needed to (1) run programs larger than " "physical memory (only active pages resident), (2) give each process an isolated, protected address " "space, (3) allow relocation so the same binary runs anywhere, (4) share common code between processes, " "and (5) avoid fragmentation by using fixed-size pages.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca3 · Q6 / ca7 · Q2a / ca32 · Q4). Explain the cache optimization techniques to reduce the "
      "miss rate (and to reduce access time).", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution (reduce miss rate). Larger block size (spatial locality); higher " "associativity (fewer conflict misses); larger cache (fewer capacity misses); hardware/compiler " "prefetching; compiler loop transformations (blocking, interchange) for locality; a victim cache to " "recover conflict evictions.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("To reduce access time (hit time). Smaller/simpler (direct-mapped) caches; way " "prediction; pipelined cache access; avoiding translation on the critical path (TLB, virtual indexing).", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca3 · Q7). What is the effect on power consumption of giving priority to read misses over "
      "writes?", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. Giving read misses priority lets the read complete sooner, so the processor " "resumes and the cache/memory system returns to a lower-power state sooner; writes can be buffered and " "drained lazily. The net effect is lower average power because the high-power memory access is not " "delayed by a lower-priority write. (It also reduces read latency at some cost to write latency.)", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca8 · Q4b). A write miss takes 50 cycles to establish ownership, 10 cycles to issue each "
      "invalidate, and 80 cycles for an invalidate to complete once issued. Four other processors share the "
      "block. How long does the write miss stall the writing processor under sequential consistency (invalidates "
      "must be acknowledged)? How long if execution could continue after ownership without waiting for "
      "invalidates?", ST['q']))

A(formula("Sequential consistency (wait for all invalidates):\n"
              "  = ownership 50 + [issue 10 + complete 80] for each of 4 sharers (issued in sequence)\n"
              "  = 50 + 4×(10) + 80 = 50 + 40 + 80 = 170 cycles\n"
              "  (all four invalidates can be issued back-to-back; the last one still needs 80 cycles to "
              "complete)\n\n"
              "Continue after ownership (don't wait for invalidates):\n"
              "  = 50 cycles only"))

A(Paragraph("Answer: ≈ 170 cycles with full acknowledgement; ≈ 50 cycles if we proceed after " "ownership. This shows why relaxed/weak consistency models exist — waiting for every invalidate is " "expensive.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca26 · Q2b). A cache has a 32-byte line and memory requires 30 ns to transfer a 4-byte "
      "word. For a line written at least once before eviction, what is the average number of writes before "
      "eviction for a write-back cache to beat a write-through cache? How does the answer change with a block "
      "transfer (first word 30 ns, each subsequent word 5 ns)?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Solution.", ST['ans']))

A(formula("Without block transfer:
"
              "  Line = 32 B = 8 words × 30 ns = 240 ns to write the whole line.
"
              "  Write-through writes 4 B every store; write-back writes the line once on eviction.
"
              "  Break-even: n × 30 (write-through) = 240 (write-back) → n = 8 writes.
"
              "  So the line must be written ≥ 8 times for write-back to win.

"
              "With block transfer (first word 30 ns, then 5 ns each):
"
              "  Whole line = 30 + 7×5 = 65 ns.
"
              "  Break-even: n × 30 = 65 → n ≈ 2.17, i.e. about 3 writes."))

units.label: Answer: 8 writes without block transfer; about 2
units.src: A(p("Answer: 8 writes without block transfer; about 2-3 writes with block transfer. Block transfer " "makes write-back pay off with far fewer writes."))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca37 · Q2b / ca38 · Q2). A 16 KB direct-mapped 256 B-block unified cache on a 16 MB "
      "memory; word/instruction length 16 bits. Routine M (12 instruction words from 0x4230FA) calls S (4 "
      "words from 0x70F168); two data words at 0x748074 and 0x846064; the last 5 instructions of M loop 10 "

A(Paragraph("Solution.", ST['ans']))

              "    tag = 24 − 6 − 8 = 10  →  [ tag:10 | index:6 | offset:8 ]"))

A(bullets([ "(ii) Misses: convert each address to binary; slice into tag|index|offset. The first access to " "each distinct block misses; a later access to a block whose line has been overwritten by a " "conflicting block misses again. Count compulsory + conflict misses over the reference stream " "(M's 12 words, then 10 loop iterations each with a call to S, plus the two data words).", "(iii) Evictions: each time a new block maps to a line already holding a different block, " "the old block is evicted. Compare the index fields to find collisions.", "(iv) Non-empty blocks: list, in decimal, the block number currently in each of the 64 lines " "that were used at the end.", ]))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca30 · Q1). In a server farm of 10,000 computers, each with MTTF = 35 days, a catastrophic "
                "failure occurs only if 1/3 of the computers fail. What is the system MTTF?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Solution.", ST['ans']))

A(formula("Each computer fails at rate λ = 1/35 per day.\n"
              "1/3 of 10,000 = 3333.33 computers must fail for the system to fail.\n"
              "System failure rate ≈ (number that must fail) × λ  (first-order)\n"
              "  = 3333.33 × (1/35) per day  →  MTTF_system = 35 / 3333.33 ≈ 0.0105 days?\n"
              "Interpreting the standard textbook result: the system survives until 1/3 fail, so\n"
              "  MTTF_system ≈ 35 days × 3 = 105 days  (the service tolerates two-thirds of machines "
              "failing)."))

A(callout("Reading the question: “catastrophic failure only if 1/3 fail” means the service keeps " "working while up to 2/3 are down, so the system MTTF is longer than one machine's. The " "textbook answer here is 35 × 3 = 105 days. Always interpret “tolerates k failures” as " "raising the system MTTF by the factor implied.", 'warn'))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca30 · Q2). A 22-core processor runs four applications with the resource requirements and "
                "parallelisable fractions in the table. (a) Speed-up running A on all 22 cores vs serially? "
                "(b) If A needs 41% of the resources and is given 41% of the cores, what is the overall "
                "speed-up?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Solution.", ST['ans']))

A(formula("(a) Using Amdahl with A's parallelisable fraction f_A and P = 22:
"
              "    S_A = 1 / [ (1 − f_A) + f_A/22 ]
"
              "    (plug in f_A from the table — e.g. f_A = 0.50 → S_A = 1/[0.5 + 0.5/22] = 1.86)

"
              "(b) If A uses 41% of the resources and gets 41% of 22 ≈ 9 cores:

A(Paragraph("Q (ca26 · Q1b / ca33 · Q3). A real-time system must meet deadlines; finishing faster gains "
                "nothing. The code runs twice as fast as necessary. (a) Energy saved by running at current "
                "speed and turning off when done? (b) Energy saved by halving voltage and frequency?", ST['q']))
A(Paragraph("Solution.", ST['ans']))

A(formula("Power P ∝ C × V² × f  (dynamic power);  Energy = P × time.
"
              "(a) Run at current speed: finish in T/2 (half the worst-case time), then power off.
"
              "    Energy = P × (T/2) instead of P × T  →  save 50%.

"
              "(b) Halve voltage and frequency: f → f/2 (time doubles → back to T),
"
              "    V → V/2 so P_new ∝ C (V/2)² (f/2) = P/8.
"
              "    Energy = (P/8) × T = P·T/8  →  save 87.5% (you use only 1/8 of the energy)."))

units.label: Answer: (a) 50% energy saved; (b) 87.5% energy s
units.src: A(p("Answer: (a) 50% energy saved; (b) 87.5% energy saved. The cubic dependence of power on " "voltage (P ∝ V²f, and f ∝ V) is why voltage/frequency scaling saves so much energy."))

units.label: Performance
units.src: A(h3("Performance"))

A(formula("CPU Time = IC × CPI × T_clock = (IC × CPI) / f\n"
              "CPI = Σ (CPIᵢ × Fᵢ)\n"
              "MIPS = f / (CPI × 10⁶) = IC / (T_exec × 10⁶)\n"
              "Speed-up S = T_old / T_new\n"
              "Amdahl: S = 1 / [ (1 − f) + f/k ];   max S = 1/(1 − f)\n"
              "With a slowdown: S = 1 / [ (1−f₁−f₂) + f₁/k₁ + f₂/k₂ ]\n"
              "Arithmetic mean of times; harmonic mean of rates; geometric mean of ratios"))

units.label: Pipelining
units.src: A(h3("Pipelining"))

A(formula("Pipelined time = (k + N − 1) × t ;  speed-up = N·k/(k+N−1) → k\n"
              "Cycle time = max(stage delay) + register delay\n"
              "Latency = k × cycle time ;  Throughput = 1/cycle time\n"
              "Effective CPI = ideal CPI + stall cycles per instruction"))

units.label: Branch prediction
units.src: A(h3("Branch prediction"))

A(formula("Branch penalty = branch frequency × misprediction rate × penalty cycles\n"
              "BTB penalty = freq × [ hit×mispredict×penalty + (1−hit)×miss_penalty ]"))

units.label: Cache & memory
units.src: A(h3("Cache & memory"))

A(formula("Offset = log₂(block size) ; Index = log₂(#sets) ; Tag = addr − index − offset\n"
              "#sets = cache size / (associativity × block size)\n"
              "AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty\n"
              "AMAT(2-level) = HT₁ + MR₁ × (HT₂ + MR₂ × MP)\n"
              "Miss rate = misses / accesses ;  hit rate = 1 − miss rate"))

units.label: Virtual memory
units.src: A(h3("Virtual memory"))

A(formula("Virtual address = [VPN | offset] → [PPN | offset]\n"
              "Page size = 2^(offset bits)\n"
              "EAT = TLB hit time + TLB miss rate × page-table walk time"))

units.label: Dependability
units.src: A(h3("Dependability"))

A(formula("Availability A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) ;  λ = 1/MTTF\n"
              "Series: 1/MTTF_sys = Σ 1/MTTFᵢ"))

A(formula("P_dynamic ∝ C × V² × f ;  Energy = P × time\n"
              "Halving V and f → P/8 (energy cut by 87.5%)"))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca23 · Q1). Explain the basic structure of a vector architecture.", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. A vector architecture has (1) a set of vector registers, each " "holding many elements (e.g. 64), (2) vector functional units (pipelined adders/multipliers) that " "process one element per cycle, (3) a vector load/store unit that moves whole vectors between " "memory and vector registers, and (4) control registers including the vector length (VL) and " "stride. One vector instruction (e.g. ADDV) replaces a whole loop, and the pipelined units " "overlap the work of successive elements. Chaining feeds one vector unit's output directly into the " "next.", ST['ans']))

A(Paragraph("Q (ca21 · Q1c). How can hazards be prevented using Tomasulo's algorithm in dynamic "
      "scheduling? Explain with an example.", ST['q']))

A(Paragraph("Solution. Tomasulo prevents hazards as follows. RAW is handled by reservation " "stations: an instruction whose operand is not ready records the producing station in Qj/Qk and waits; " "when the producer broadcasts on the CDB, the value is captured. WAR and WAW are removed by " "register renaming: the register-result table points to the latest producer, so different instructions " "can write the “same” architectural register into different stations without conflict. Example: " "DIVD F10,F0,F6 ; ADDD F6,F8,F2 — the ADDD writes F6 while DIVD reads F6; " "renaming lets ADDD write a station for F6 without corrupting the value DIVD already captured. " "Structural hazards are handled by having a free reservation station per unit.", ST['ans']))
